concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: An audit conducted under the Standards on Auditing obtains reasonable assurance, which is a high level of assurance but not absolute assurance.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: The preconditions for an audit are an acceptable financial reporting framework and management's agreement to the premise on which an audit is conducted — its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access and information. Where the preconditions are not present, the auditor does not accept the engagement.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: Where management imposes a limitation on scope before the engagement is accepted, and the auditor expects that limitation will result in a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor does not accept the engagement unless law or regulation requires it.

concepts.subsection: SA 220 (Revised) — Quality Management for an Audit
concepts.statement: The engagement partner takes overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement. Work may be delegated across the engagement team, but the responsibility for quality is not delegated with it.

concepts.subsection: SA 230 — Audit Documentation
concepts.statement: The final audit file is assembled ordinarily within not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: Management override of controls is a significant risk presumed to be present in every audit, and it is not rebuttable.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: There is a presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition, and unlike management override that presumption may be rebutted with documented reasons.

concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: SA 250 splits laws into two categories, and the auditor's responsibility differs between them. For laws with a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance. For other laws that are fundamental to the operating aspects of the business, the auditor only performs specified procedures to help identify non-compliance.

concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: The auditor communicates the planned scope and timing of the audit to those charged with governance, not only the findings.

concepts.subsection: SA 265 — Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control
concepts.statement: Significant deficiencies in internal control are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis.

concepts.subsection: SA 299 (Revised) — Joint Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to that auditor, and all joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible for the work not divided.

concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement
concepts.statement: A significant risk is one requiring special audit consideration, and for such risks the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's related controls.

concepts.subsection: SA 320 — Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit
concepts.statement: Performance materiality is set below materiality for the financial statements as a whole, to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements aggregate above materiality.

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: When the auditor has determined that an assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level is a significant risk, substantive procedures specifically responsive to that risk must be performed.

concepts.subsection: SA 402 — Audit Considerations Relating to an Entity Using a Service Organisation
concepts.statement: A Type 1 report describes the service organisation's system and the design of its controls at a point in time. A Type 2 report also reports on their operating effectiveness over a period. Only a Type 2 report can give evidence about operating effectiveness.

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: Uncorrected misstatements are communicated to those charged with governance and the auditor evaluates whether they are material individually or in aggregate.

concepts.subsection: SA 500 — Audit Evidence
concepts.statement: Sufficiency is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence; appropriateness is the measure of its quality, being its relevance and its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations for Selected Items
concepts.statement: When inventory is material to the financial statements, the auditor must attend the physical inventory counting unless it is impracticable.

concepts.subsection: SA 505 — External Confirmations
concepts.statement: Negative confirmations may be used as the sole substantive procedure only when the assessed risk is low, the population is large and homogeneous, a very low exception rate is expected, and the auditor is not aware of circumstances that would cause recipients to disregard them.

concepts.subsection: SA 510 — Initial Audit Engagements: Opening Balances
concepts.statement: In an initial audit engagement the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements, and whether accounting policies reflected in the opening balances have been consistently applied.

concepts.subsection: SA 520 — Analytical Procedures
concepts.statement: Analytical procedures are mandatory at two points in an audit — as risk assessment procedures during planning, and near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion. Using them as substantive procedures is optional, a choice the auditor makes about how to respond to an assessed risk.

concepts.subsection: SA 530 — Audit Sampling
concepts.statement: Misstatements found in a sample are projected to the population the sample was drawn from. The sample is a means of reaching a conclusion about the whole population, so the error found in it is evidence about the whole population, not only about the items examined.

concepts.subsection: SA 550 — Related Parties
concepts.statement: A significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business gives rise to a significant risk. The auditor inspects the underlying contracts and evaluates whether the business rationale suggests the transaction was entered into to engage in fraudulent financial reporting or to conceal misappropriation of assets.

concepts.subsection: SA 560 — Subsequent Events
concepts.statement: Where the report is amended for a subsequent event, dual dating confines the auditor's responsibility for events after the original date to that amendment alone.

concepts.subsection: SA 570 (Revised) — Going Concern
concepts.statement: Where a material uncertainty about going concern exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is unmodified and a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" is included.

concepts.subsection: SA 580 — Written Representations
concepts.statement: Written representations are audit evidence, but they are not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters they deal with. Obtaining them does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains.

concepts.subsection: SA 600 — Using the Work of Another Auditor
concepts.statement: Where a principal auditor uses the work of another auditor for a component, the principal auditor states the division of responsibility in the audit report, naming the magnitude of the portion audited by the other auditor. The principal auditor is not responsible for the work entrusted to the other auditor.

concepts.subsection: SA 610 (Revised) — Using the Work of Internal Auditors
concepts.statement: SA 610 (Revised) as issued in India does not permit the external auditor to use internal auditors to provide direct assistance; the work of the internal audit function may still be used.

citation.ref: para 5 and the Indian scope limitation

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: The auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion, and that responsibility is not reduced by using the work of an auditor's expert. The auditor's report does not refer to the expert unless the reference is required by law or regulation, and where it is, the report must state that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: The auditor's report opens with the Opinion section, and the Basis for Opinion section comes directly after it. The conclusion is stated before the reasons for it, so a reader who stops after the first paragraph has still read the opinion.

concepts.subsection: SA 701 — Communicating Key Audit Matters
concepts.statement: Key audit matters are required for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and where otherwise required by law or voluntarily undertaken.

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: A material misstatement that is not pervasive gives a qualified opinion; a material misstatement that is pervasive gives an adverse opinion.

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements; an Other Matter paragraph refers to a matter not so disclosed but relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report.

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — Comparative Information: Corresponding Figures and Comparative Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Where comparatives are presented as corresponding figures, the auditor's opinion refers to the current period only and does not refer to the corresponding figures. Where they are presented as comparative financial statements, the opinion refers to each period for which financial statements are presented.

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: The auditor reads the other information in the annual report and considers whether it is materially inconsistent with the financial statements or with the auditor's knowledge obtained in the audit. The auditor does not audit the other information and expresses no opinion or conclusion on it.

items.stem: What level of assurance does an audit conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing obtain?

options.text: Reasonable assurance, which is a high but not absolute level of assurance
options.why: SA 200 defines the auditor's objective as obtaining reasonable assurance — a high level, but not absolute, because of the inherent limitations of an audit: the nature of financial reporting, the nature of audit procedures, and the need to complete the audit at a reasonable cost within a reasonable time.

options.text: Absolute assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement
options.misconception: promises absolute assurance, which no audit can give
options.why: Absolute assurance is unattainable. SA 200 states the inherent limitations expressly: audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive, and testing is selective rather than exhaustive.

options.text: A stated numerical probability that the financial statements are free from material misstatement
options.misconception: treats assurance as a probability the auditor is required to quantify
options.why: The Standards nowhere ask the auditor to express assurance as a percentage. Reasonable assurance is a qualitative concept about the sufficiency of evidence obtained, not a computed figure.

options.text: Moderate assurance, since "reasonable" means something less than high
options.misconception: reads "reasonable" as a lowering of the standard rather than a description of a high one
options.why: SA 200 uses "reasonable" to mean high. Moderate or limited assurance is the language of review engagements under SRE 2400, not of an audit.

items.stem: Can you accept the engagement?

options.text: No, because management's agreement to its responsibilities is a precondition for an audit
options.why: The premise of an audit is that management acknowledges its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control, and for providing access and information. Without that acknowledgement there is nothing for the audit to be an audit of, so SA 210 does not permit acceptance.

options.text: Yes, provided the audit report is modified to say management did not accept responsibility
options.misconception: converts a refusal to accept into a reporting matter
options.why: A modification describes the result of an audit that was performed. SA 210 stops the engagement earlier, at acceptance, precisely so the auditor is never in the position of reporting on an audit that lacked its foundation.

options.text: Yes, because the size of the company makes formal internal control unnecessary
options.misconception: confuses how elaborate the controls are with whether responsibility is accepted
options.why: The precondition is about who is responsible, not about how sophisticated the controls are. A small entity's controls may be simple; management still has to acknowledge them as its own.

options.text: Yes, if the promoter gives the acknowledgement orally instead
options.misconception: treats an oral acknowledgement as satisfying a written agreement of terms
options.why: SA 210 requires the agreed terms to be recorded in an engagement letter or other suitable written agreement. An oral assurance leaves nothing that can be pointed to later.

items.scenario: A prospective client asks you to audit its financial statements but says it will not sign any acknowledgement of responsibility for internal control, on the ground that the company is small and the promoter handles everything personally.

items.stem: What should you do?

options.text: Decline the engagement, because the limitation would lead to a disclaimer of opinion
options.why: The two areas closed off are 70 per cent of total assets, so the auditor could not obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about anything material. SA 210 does not allow accepting an engagement whose known limitation will end in a disclaimer, unless law requires it.

options.text: Accept, perform what you can, and issue a disclaimer of opinion
options.misconception: accepts a doomed engagement on the basis that the report will say so
options.why: Knowingly accepting an audit that cannot produce an opinion lends the auditor's name to an exercise with no outcome. That is the outcome SA 210 exists to prevent, which is why the test is applied at acceptance.

options.text: Accept, and use alternative procedures instead of confirmation and attendance
options.misconception: assumes alternative procedures can always replace a blocked procedure
options.why: Alternative procedures address a limitation the auditor meets during the audit, and they work only when they can actually produce the evidence. Here the restriction is imposed in advance and covers most of the balance sheet.

options.text: Accept, and report the restriction to those charged with governance
options.misconception: substitutes communication for the acceptance decision
options.why: Those charged with governance are, in this scenario, the source of the restriction. Reporting it back to them does not obtain the evidence or discharge the SA 210 test.

items.scenario: Before appointing you, a company tells you that you may not circularise trade receivables or attend the inventory count, because both would disturb its customers and its plant. Receivables and inventory together are 70 per cent of total assets.

items.stem: Where does responsibility for the quality of this engagement sit?

options.text: With the engagement partner, who retains overall responsibility however the work is delegated
options.why: SA 220 (Revised) places overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement partner. Delegating review work is normal and expected; delegating the responsibility for quality is not possible.

options.text: With the manager, who performed the detailed review
options.misconception: moves responsibility to whoever did the work
options.why: The manager is accountable within the firm for the review performed, but the standard does not shift the engagement partner's overall responsibility onto the person delegated to.

options.text: With the firm, through its system of quality management
options.misconception: substitutes the firm-level system for the engagement-level responsibility
options.why: The firm's system is a separate requirement under SQM 1 and sits alongside this one. It supports the engagement partner rather than replacing them.

options.text: Shared equally between the engagement partner and the engagement quality reviewer
options.misconception: treats an independent review as a transfer of responsibility
options.why: An engagement quality review is an objective evaluation of significant judgements. It does not reduce or share the engagement partner's overall responsibility for quality.

items.scenario: An audit is staffed with a manager, two seniors and three articles. The engagement partner visits the client twice, reviews the summary memorandum and signs the report. The detailed review of every working paper was done by the manager.

items.stem: Within what period must the final audit file ordinarily be assembled after the auditor's report is dated?

options.text: 60 days
options.why: SA 230 sets an outer limit of ordinarily not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report for completing the administrative assembly of the final file.

options.text: 30 days
options.misconception: carries over a shorter statutory filing period as if it governed file assembly
options.why: No provision of SA 230 sets 30 days. The number is imported from unrelated filing deadlines.

options.text: 90 days
options.misconception: confuses assembly with the longer periods that govern retention
options.why: Retention runs for years, not 90 days; assembly is the 60-day requirement. The two are separate obligations under SA 230.

options.text: Before the auditor's report is signed
options.misconception: treats assembly as a precondition to signing rather than an administrative step after it
options.why: SA 230 measures the period from the date of the auditor's report, which presupposes the report is already dated. Assembly is administrative and adds no new evidence.

items.stem: What does SA 230 require when you add to the file after the report date?

options.text: Document when and by whom the addition was made and reviewed, and why it was made
options.why: Additions during the assembly period are allowed — assembling the file is administrative. What SA 230 requires is that the change be visible: the reasons for it, and who made and reviewed it and when, so the file cannot be quietly rewritten after the event.

options.text: Nothing, provided the addition is made within sixty days of the report date
options.misconception: treats the assembly period as a window in which changes need no record
options.why: The period bounds when assembly must finish. It does not suspend the documentation requirement for changes made inside it.

options.text: Nothing may be added after the report date, so the paper must be left out
options.misconception: reads the assembly period as a freeze on the file
options.why: The file is assembled after the report is signed; that is what the assembly period is for. The rule governs how additions are recorded, not whether they may be made.

options.text: The audit report must be reissued to reflect the additional documentation
options.misconception: confuses completing the file with changing the opinion
options.why: Writing up a discussion that informed an opinion already reached changes nothing about the opinion. Reissuing a report is for facts discovered after the date that would have changed it.

items.scenario: Two weeks after signing the audit report, you realise a working paper recording your discussion with the finance director about a provision was never filed. You write it up now and add it to the file.

items.stem: How should you treat the risk of management override of controls?

options.text: As a significant risk present in every audit, so the required responses are performed regardless of the control environment
options.why: SA 240 requires the auditor to treat management override as a significant risk in all audits. Management is uniquely placed to override controls that otherwise operate effectively, so a strong control environment does not remove the risk — it is precisely what management is able to override.

options.text: As a significant risk only where the assessment shows the control environment to be weak
options.misconception: makes a mandatory risk conditional on the strength of controls
options.why: SA 240 attaches no such condition. The risk arises from management's position of authority, not from any deficiency in the controls it is able to override.

options.text: As a presumption that may be rebutted with documented reasons, as with revenue recognition
options.misconception: borrows the rebuttable revenue presumption and applies it where the Standard allows no rebuttal
options.why: SA 240 makes only the revenue-recognition fraud risk rebuttable. The management-override requirement is stated unconditionally and there is no mechanism in the Standard for setting it aside.

options.text: As a significant risk only in the audits of listed entities
options.misconception: confines a requirement that applies to all audits to listed entities alone
options.why: SA 240 draws no distinction by class of entity here. If anything the risk is higher in owner-managed entities, where fewer people stand between management and the accounting records.

items.scenario: A client has a well-designed control environment, no history of fraud, and an audit committee that meets regularly. Your engagement team argues that testing journal entries for management override adds nothing this year.

items.stem: What is the status of the presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition?

options.text: It is presumed, but the auditor may rebut it and must document the reasons for that conclusion
options.why: SA 240 requires the auditor to presume fraud risks in revenue recognition, while permitting rebuttal where the presumption is not applicable in the circumstances. Where it is rebutted, the Standard requires the reasons to be documented.

options.text: It cannot be rebutted in any circumstances
options.misconception: makes the revenue presumption as absolute as the management-override requirement
options.why: SA 240 phrases the two differently on purpose. Revenue is rebuttable in the circumstances of the engagement; management override is not.

options.text: It applies uniformly to every revenue stream, so no analysis of which streams carry the risk is needed
options.misconception: applies the presumption as a blanket rule instead of identifying which revenue assertions carry the risk
options.why: SA 240 requires the auditor to identify which types of revenue, revenue transactions or assertions give rise to the risk. A blanket assumption skips the identification the Standard asks for.

options.text: It may be rebutted only with the approval of those charged with governance
options.misconception: makes a professional judgement subject to a governance approval the Standard never requires
options.why: The rebuttal is the auditor's judgement, documented in the working papers. SA 240 requires documentation, not consent.

items.stem: Why does SA 240 require you to test journal entries in every audit, and what makes these ones urgent?

options.text: Because management can override controls that otherwise operate effectively, and these entries carry the hallmarks of override
options.why: SA 240 treats management override as a risk present in every entity, however good the controls, because the people who can override them are the people who run them. Testing journal entries is one of the required responses. These entries carry the classic markers — posted at the period end, outside the normal process, approved by one person, and explained by a narration that explains nothing.

options.text: Because journal entries are always the largest source of error in any accounting system
options.misconception: justifies the procedure by frequency of error rather than by the override risk
options.why: The requirement is not about where errors happen most. It exists because override is the one risk that cannot be controlled away, since it is the controls themselves that are being overridden.

options.text: It is not required in every audit; it is required only where fraud risk factors have been identified
options.misconception: makes a mandatory response conditional on identifying risk factors first
options.why: SA 240 requires the journal entry testing regardless. Management override is presumed to be a risk in every entity, so the response is not conditional on anything being spotted first.

options.text: Because the auditor is required to detect all fraud, and journals are where fraud is hidden
options.misconception: overstates the auditor's responsibility from reasonable assurance to detection of all fraud
options.why: The auditor obtains reasonable assurance that the statements are free from material misstatement, whether from fraud or error. That is not a duty to detect all fraud, and SA 240 does not create one.

items.scenario: A company posts 41 manual journal entries on 31 March 2026, all after the normal cut-off, all approved by the chief financial officer alone, and all with the narration "regrouping". Their net effect increases profit by ₹3.7 crore.

items.stem: What is your responsibility under SA 250 for compliance with the environmental clearance?

options.text: Perform specified procedures to help identify non-compliance, without obtaining evidence about compliance itself
options.why: The clearance is fundamental to the operating aspects of the business but has no direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, so it falls in SA 250's second category. There the auditor's responsibility is limited to specified procedures — enquiring of management and inspecting correspondence with the relevant licensing authority — rather than obtaining evidence about compliance.

options.text: Obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance with every condition
options.misconception: applies the higher first-category duty to a law with no direct effect on the figures
options.why: That is the duty for the first category only — laws that directly determine material amounts and disclosures. Extending it to every law fundamental to operations would make the auditor a compliance inspector, which SA 250 expressly does not do.

options.text: No responsibility at all, because compliance with environmental law is management's concern
options.misconception: reads the split as duty versus no duty, rather than two different duties
options.why: Both categories carry a duty. The second is narrower, not absent: SA 250 still requires enquiry of management and inspection of correspondence with the licensing authority.

options.text: Report the matter to the regulator before completing the audit
options.misconception: jumps to external reporting before the standard's own procedures
options.why: Reporting outside the entity is a separate question that arises only after non-compliance is identified or suspected, and is governed by law and by SA 250's later paragraphs. It is not the auditor's responsibility for compliance as such.

items.scenario: You are auditing a chemical manufacturer. The company holds an environmental clearance whose conditions govern how effluent is discharged. Breaching those conditions can lead to the plant being shut down, but the clearance does not itself determine any figure recognised in the financial statements.

items.stem: Which of these must be communicated to those charged with governance?

options.text: The planned scope and timing of the audit
options.why: SA 260 (Revised) requires the auditor to communicate an overview of the planned scope and timing of the audit. Communication runs in both directions and before the work as well as after it, so that governance understands what the audit will and will not cover.

options.text: Only the findings from the audit, since scope is the auditor's own affair
options.misconception: restricts the communication to findings when the Standard also requires planning matters
options.why: SA 260 (Revised) lists the auditor's responsibilities, the planned scope and timing, and significant findings as separate required communications. Reporting only findings omits two of the three.

options.text: Nothing, unless the entity is listed
options.misconception: treats a requirement that applies to all audits as one confined to listed entities
options.why: Only the independence communication in SA 260 (Revised) is confined to listed entities. Scope and timing are communicated in every audit.

options.text: Nothing further, provided the matters have been discussed with management
options.misconception: treats management as a substitute for those charged with governance
options.why: The two are different bodies with different roles, and they overlap only in some entities. SA 260 (Revised) addresses the communication to those charged with governance specifically.

items.stem: What does SA 265 require you to do?

options.text: Communicate the three significant deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis
options.why: SA 265 requires significant deficiencies to be communicated in writing and on a timely basis to those charged with governance. The written form exists so that the matter is recorded and can be acted on; timeliness exists so it can be acted on while it still matters.

options.text: Communicate the three significant deficiencies orally at the closing meeting
options.misconception: substitutes an oral communication where the Standard requires writing
options.why: SA 265 specifies written communication for significant deficiencies. An oral briefing may supplement it but cannot replace it.

options.text: Communicate all eleven deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance
options.misconception: raises every deficiency to the level the Standard reserves for significant ones
options.why: Only significant deficiencies go in writing to those charged with governance. Other deficiencies of sufficient importance go to management, at the appropriate level.

options.text: Communicate the three significant deficiencies to management alone
options.misconception: stops at management where the Standard requires the communication to reach governance
options.why: SA 265 directs significant deficiencies to those charged with governance. Communicating only to management withholds them from the body responsible for overseeing management.

items.scenario: During the audit you identify eleven deficiencies in internal control. Three are significant deficiencies in your professional judgement; the remaining eight are minor.

items.stem: Who bears responsibility for that misstatement?

options.text: Firm A alone, because the northern division was the work divided to it; both firms remain jointly and severally responsible for the undivided treasury work
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) makes each joint auditor responsible for the work allocated to that auditor, and all joint auditors jointly and severally responsible for work not divided and for decisions taken together, including the audit report.

options.text: Both firms jointly, because joint auditors are responsible for the whole audit without division
options.misconception: collapses divided work into joint responsibility and leaves division of work with no meaning
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) provides expressly for division of work and attaches individual responsibility to it. If everything were joint, the Standard's division provisions would do nothing.

options.text: Firm A alone, and no element of the audit carries joint responsibility
options.misconception: removes the joint element entirely and leaves undivided work unowned
options.why: The undivided work — here the treasury operations, and the report itself — is jointly and severally the responsibility of both. Individual responsibility exists alongside joint responsibility, not instead of it.

options.text: The firm that signs first, as the principal joint auditor
options.misconception: invents a principal joint auditor, a rank SA 299 does not create
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) recognises no hierarchy among joint auditors. Order of signature carries no consequence for responsibility.

items.scenario: Two firms are joint auditors of a company. The work is divided by division: Firm A takes the northern division, Firm B the southern. Neither firm's division covers the group's treasury operations, which both firms address together. A misstatement is later found in the northern division's revenue.

items.stem: What follows from determining that an identified risk is a significant risk?

options.text: It requires special audit consideration, and the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's controls relevant to that risk
options.why: SA 315 (Revised) defines a significant risk as one requiring special audit consideration, and requires the auditor to evaluate the design and determine the implementation of the controls relevant to it. Understanding those controls is what makes a targeted response possible.

options.text: Every high-value balance is a significant risk, so materiality alone identifies them
options.misconception: reduces a judgement about the nature of a risk to the size of the balance
options.why: SA 315 (Revised) points to complexity, subjectivity, significant judgement, unusual transactions and related-party dealings — none of which is measured in rupees. A large but routine balance may carry no significant risk at all.

options.text: Significant risks arise only from fraud
options.misconception: confines significant risks to fraud when error can equally produce one
options.why: Fraud risks are always significant risks, but the category is wider. Complex estimates and unusual transactions give rise to significant risks of error.

options.text: They may be addressed by substantive procedures alone, with no need to understand the related controls
options.misconception: skips the mandatory understanding of controls by going straight to substantive work
options.why: SA 315 (Revised) requires the understanding of related controls whatever the planned response. The response is a separate question, governed by SA 330.

items.stem: Why does this transaction give rise to a significant risk?

options.text: It is an unusual related party transaction outside the normal course of business, with a significant effect on the reported result
options.why: SA 315 (Revised) points to unusual transactions and related-party dealings as indicators. Every indicator is present at once here: the counterparty is related, the transaction is outside normal operations, its timing is close to the year end, and it changes the headline result.

options.text: Because the gain is large in rupee terms
options.misconception: reduces a judgement about the nature of a risk to the size of the amount
options.why: Size alone does not make a significant risk. A large but routine sale carries none. What matters here is that the transaction is related-party, non-routine and result-changing.

options.text: Because the company is listed, and all listed company transactions carry significant risk
options.misconception: attaches the risk to the entity's status rather than to the transaction
options.why: Listing brings its own reporting and independence requirements, but it does not make every transaction a significant risk. The assessment is made transaction by transaction.

options.text: It does not; a completed sale supported by a registered deed is fully verifiable
options.misconception: mistakes ease of vouching for absence of risk
options.why: The deed proves a sale occurred. It says nothing about whether the price was arm's length, whether the substance matches the form, or whether the timing was chosen to produce the result — which is where the risk lives.

items.scenario: A listed company sells one of its two factories to an entity owned by the managing director's brother, three weeks before the year end, at a gain that turns a loss into a profit.

items.stem: Why is performance materiality set below materiality for the financial statements as a whole?

options.text: To reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements together exceed materiality
options.why: SA 320 sets performance materiality to absorb aggregation risk. Individually immaterial misstatements can add up past materiality, and some misstatements will go undetected, so the working threshold has to sit below the reporting one.

options.text: It does not: performance materiality is the same amount as materiality for the financial statements as a whole
options.misconception: equates the two amounts and leaves nothing to absorb aggregation risk
options.why: If the two were equal, a set of individually tolerable misstatements could aggregate above materiality and pass unnoticed. SA 320 requires the lower amount for that reason.

options.text: It is the threshold above which misstatements are reported to those charged with governance
options.misconception: confuses performance materiality with the clearly trivial threshold used for accumulating misstatements
options.why: The threshold for accumulating and reporting misstatements is a different figure under SA 450. Performance materiality governs the extent of procedures, not what gets reported.

options.text: It is set at the engagement partner's preference, without reference to aggregation
options.misconception: treats the amount as unconstrained preference rather than a judgement directed at a stated objective
options.why: SA 320 states the objective the amount must serve and points to the factors bearing on it — understanding of the entity, the nature of misstatements found in previous audits. Judgement operates within that, not outside it.

items.stem: What does SA 320 require you to do?

options.text: Revise materiality, and reconsider whether the nature, timing and extent of further procedures remain appropriate
options.why: Materiality is revised when the auditor becomes aware of information that would have led to a different figure initially. A drop from ₹16 crore to ₹6 crore is exactly that. Revising the number is only half of it — the audit plan built on the old number has to be revisited too.

options.text: Keep the planning figure, since materiality is set at planning and changing it undermines the plan
options.misconception: treats materiality as fixed once set
options.why: SA 320 provides for revision precisely because circumstances change during an audit. Holding to ₹80 lakh against a ₹6 crore result would let misstatements of over 13 per cent of profit pass untested.

options.text: Revise materiality, but leave the planned procedures unchanged to preserve comparability
options.misconception: revises the number without revising anything that depends on it
options.why: Sample sizes, scoping and the threshold for accumulating misstatements all follow from materiality. Changing it and leaving them alone leaves the audit executed to the old figure.

options.text: Use the original figure for work already performed and the revised figure only for work still to come
options.misconception: applies two materialities to one set of financial statements
options.why: One set of financial statements has one materiality. Work already done has to be reconsidered against the revised figure, not left standing against a threshold now known to be wrong.

items.scenario: You set materiality for the financial statements as a whole at ₹80 lakh during planning, based on forecast profit before tax of ₹16 crore. In February the company loses its largest customer and the actual profit before tax comes in at ₹6 crore.

items.stem: What does SA 330 require of your response?

options.text: Substantive procedures specifically responsive to that risk must still be performed
options.why: SA 330 requires substantive procedures specifically responsive to every risk assessed as significant, whatever the results of controls testing. Effective controls reduce the extent of substantive work; they never remove the requirement to do some.

options.text: Effective controls testing alone is a sufficient response to a significant risk
options.misconception: lets controls testing discharge a requirement the Standard states separately
options.why: SA 330 states the substantive requirement independently of controls testing precisely so that it cannot be discharged by controls alone.

options.text: Substantive analytical procedures alone are sufficient for a significant risk
options.misconception: meets the requirement with analytical procedures where the Standard calls for tests of details
options.why: SA 330 requires that where the approach to a significant risk consists only of substantive procedures, those procedures include tests of details. Analytics alone do not answer a risk of this kind.

options.text: The response may be deferred to the following year's audit if time is short
options.misconception: postpones a current-period requirement into a later engagement
options.why: The requirement attaches to the audit of the period under report. Nothing in SA 330 permits deferral.

items.scenario: You have assessed the valuation of a complex financial instrument as a significant risk. Controls over the valuation model are well designed and you have tested them, finding them effective.

items.stem: Can the Type 1 report support your planned reliance on those controls?

options.text: No, because it reports on the design of controls at a point in time and not on whether they operated throughout the period
options.why: Reliance on controls requires evidence that they operated effectively across the period being audited. A Type 1 report says the controls were suitably designed on one date, which leaves the other 364 days unevidenced.

options.text: Yes, because it is dated at the year end and so covers the year then ended
options.misconception: reads the report date as the period it covers
options.why: The date is the point at which design was assessed, not a period of coverage. A report dated at the year end says nothing about the eleven months before it.

options.text: Yes, provided the service auditor is independent of both the provider and your client
options.misconception: treats the service auditor's independence as the thing that makes the report sufficient
options.why: Independence and competence are necessary before the report can be used at all. They do not change what a Type 1 report contains, which is the limitation here.

options.text: No, because a report from a service auditor can never be used as audit evidence by the user auditor
options.misconception: rejects service auditor reports entirely rather than distinguishing the two types
options.why: SA 402 expressly contemplates using them. A Type 2 report would support this reliance; the problem is which type is in your hands, not the category.

items.scenario: Your client outsources its entire payroll to a service provider. You intend to rely on controls at the provider to reduce substantive testing of payroll costs. The provider gives you a Type 1 report dated 31 March 2026, the year end.

items.stem: What does SA 450 require?

options.text: Communicate the uncorrected misstatements to those charged with governance and evaluate whether they are material individually or in aggregate
options.why: SA 450 requires uncorrected misstatements to be communicated to those charged with governance, identifying them individually, along with the effect on the opinion, and requires the auditor to evaluate their materiality individually and in aggregate.

options.text: Communicate only the misstatements management corrected, since the uncorrected ones affect only the opinion
options.misconception: reverses the requirement and withholds precisely the misstatements governance needs to see
options.why: SA 450 directs the communication at uncorrected misstatements. Corrected ones may be communicated too, but the requirement runs the other way round.

options.text: Accumulate every misstatement identified, including clearly trivial ones
options.misconception: removes the clearly trivial threshold and accumulates everything
options.why: SA 450 requires accumulation of misstatements other than those that are clearly trivial, and requires the auditor to set that threshold. Accumulating everything ignores a distinction the Standard draws.

options.text: Modify the opinion, because uncorrected misstatements always require modification
options.misconception: treats any uncorrected misstatement as automatically fatal to an unmodified opinion
options.why: Modification follows from materiality, not from the mere fact of non-correction. At ₹18 lakh against materiality of ₹90 lakh, the evaluation SA 450 requires is what decides the question.

items.scenario: At the end of the audit you have accumulated misstatements of ₹18 lakh that management has declined to correct. Materiality for the financial statements as a whole is ₹90 lakh.

items.stem: How do you evaluate whether these are material?

options.text: Aggregate them, and also consider whether any one of them is material by its nature regardless of size
options.why: The three together are ₹48 lakh, above the ₹45 lakh threshold, and SA 450 requires the aggregate to be evaluated rather than each item alone. Size is not the only test either — a misstatement can be material by nature, for instance one that turns a loss into a profit or that touches a related party.

options.text: Treat each separately, and conclude none is material because none exceeds ₹45 lakh
options.misconception: evaluates misstatements one at a time when the standard requires the aggregate
options.why: This is the specific error SA 450 exists to prevent. Three misstatements, each comfortably below materiality, add to more than it, and financial statements are read as a whole rather than one adjustment at a time.

options.text: Net them off, since the overstated prepayment partly offsets the understated provision
options.misconception: nets misstatements in opposite directions without regard to what they affect
options.why: Offsetting is not automatic. These touch different balances and different assertions, and netting them would hide two errors behind each other rather than show that both exist.

options.text: Report only the largest one to those charged with governance
options.misconception: filters what is communicated by size rather than communicating the accumulation
options.why: SA 450 requires uncorrected misstatements to be communicated and their effect on the opinion explained. Reporting one of three withholds exactly the aggregate that matters.

items.scenario: You have accumulated three uncorrected misstatements: an understated provision of ₹18 lakh, an overstated prepayment of ₹9 lakh, and an unrecorded liability of ₹21 lakh. Materiality for the financial statements as a whole is ₹45 lakh. Management declines to adjust any of them.

items.stem: What is the difference between sufficiency and appropriateness of audit evidence?

options.text: Sufficiency is the measure of quantity; appropriateness is the measure of quality, being relevance and reliability
options.why: SA 500 defines the two separately and they interact: the higher the assessed risk, the more evidence is likely to be required, and the poorer its quality, the more of it may be needed. Both must be satisfied — neither alone supports an opinion.

options.text: They are two names for the same test of whether enough evidence was obtained
options.misconception: collapses two defined terms into one and loses the quality dimension
options.why: SA 500 defines them in separate sub-paragraphs because they measure different things. Quantity says nothing about whether the evidence bears on the assertion at issue.

options.text: More evidence always compensates for evidence of poor quality
options.misconception: assumes quantity can substitute for quality without limit
options.why: SA 500 notes that obtaining more evidence may not compensate for its poor quality. A large volume of unreliable evidence remains unreliable.

options.text: Appropriateness concerns only the source of the evidence, not whether it bears on the assertion
options.misconception: reduces appropriateness to reliability and drops relevance out of the definition
options.why: Appropriateness has two limbs in SA 500: relevance and reliability. Evidence from an impeccable source that addresses the wrong assertion is not appropriate.

items.stem: Which carries the greatest weight, and why?

options.text: The supplier's statement, because evidence from an independent external source is more reliable than evidence generated inside the entity
options.why: SA 500 ranks reliability partly by origin. A document obtained directly from an independent third party has not passed through the hands of the people whose figures are under audit, which is what makes it stronger than anything the entity produced itself.

options.text: The purchase ledger printout, because it is the entity's own accounting record and ties to the financial statements
options.misconception: mistakes agreement with the accounts for corroboration of them
options.why: It ties to the financial statements because it is where the financial statements came from. Agreeing a figure to its own source proves arithmetic, not existence.

options.text: The photocopied invoice, because it is the original commercial document underlying the transaction
options.misconception: values the document type while ignoring that it is a copy supplied by the client
options.why: An original invoice would be stronger than a ledger, but a photocopy handed over by the entity has both lost the safeguards of an original and travelled through the entity. SA 500 treats copies as less reliable than originals.

options.text: All three equally, since together they agree to the same amount
options.misconception: treats agreement between sources as making each of them reliable
options.why: Three sources agreeing is useful, but two of these are not independent of the entity. If the entity's records are wrong, its ledger and its photocopy will be wrong together.

items.scenario: You are verifying a trade payable of ₹2.4 crore. Three things are available: the supplier's statement sent directly to you, the client's purchase ledger printout, and a photocopy of the supplier invoice given to you by the client's accounts clerk.

items.stem: What does SA 501 require of you?

options.text: Attend the physical inventory counting, unless attendance is impracticable
options.why: SA 501 requires attendance at the physical count where inventory is material, to evaluate management's instructions, observe the count, inspect the inventory and perform test counts. Impracticability is the only exception, and inconvenience is not impracticability.

options.text: Attend the count in every audit, whether or not inventory is material
options.misconception: detaches the requirement from materiality and extends it to every engagement
options.why: The requirement in SA 501 is conditional on inventory being material to the financial statements. Where it is not, the auditor's response is governed by the ordinary risk assessment.

options.text: Obtain a certificate from management as to the quantities held, in place of attending
options.misconception: accepts a management representation in place of the auditor's own observation
options.why: A written representation is not a substitute for evidence that could reasonably be obtained directly. SA 580 says so expressly, and here the count was accessible.

options.text: Attend only in the first year of the engagement, and rely on that year thereafter
options.misconception: treats attendance as a one-time procedure rather than one required each period
options.why: The requirement attaches to each audit in which inventory is material. Quantities are re-counted each year, so last year's observation is evidence about last year's balance.

items.scenario: Inventory is ₹6 crore against a balance sheet total of ₹40 crore and is material to the financial statements. The count is held at four warehouses on 31 March, and none of them is inaccessible.

items.stem: When may negative confirmations be used as the sole substantive procedure to address an assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level?

options.text: Only when risk is low, controls are effective, the population is large and homogeneous, a very low exception rate is expected, and recipients are unlikely to disregard the request
options.why: SA 505 sets all these conditions together because a negative confirmation produces evidence only from the absence of a reply, which is weak. The conditions exist to make silence mean something.

options.text: Wherever positive confirmations could be used, since the two are interchangeable
options.misconception: treats a weaker form of evidence as equivalent to a stronger one
options.why: A positive confirmation produces evidence whether or not the balance is agreed. A negative one produces evidence only if the recipient disagrees and troubles to say so.

options.text: Freely, because a non-reply to a negative confirmation is evidence that the balance is correct
options.misconception: reads silence as agreement when it may only mean the request was ignored or never arrived
options.why: SA 505 states that unreturned negative confirmations do not explicitly provide evidence that the intended party received the request or verified it. Silence is ambiguous.

options.text: Wherever positive replies are proving slow to arrive
options.misconception: chooses the procedure for administrative convenience rather than on the conditions the Standard sets
options.why: Slow replies call for follow-up or alternative procedures. They do not alter the assessed risk or the character of the population, which are what the conditions turn on.

items.stem: What does SA 505 require you to do about the six non-replies?

options.text: Perform alternative procedures on each, such as examining subsequent receipts and the underlying despatch documents
options.why: A positive request that goes unanswered gives no evidence at all, and the balances are well above performance materiality. SA 505 requires alternative procedures to obtain relevant and reliable evidence for the balances the confirmations did not settle.

options.text: Treat the silence as agreement, because a customer who disputed the balance would have replied
options.misconception: reads a non-reply to a positive request as if it were a non-reply to a negative one
options.why: That inference belongs to negative confirmation, which is why negative confirmation is permitted only in narrow circumstances. With a positive request, silence means nothing was obtained.

options.text: Extend the sample by sending requests to twenty more customers
options.misconception: replaces evidence about specific balances with evidence about different ones
options.why: Confirming other customers says nothing about these six. The gap is in named balances totalling ₹1.6 crore, and only work on those balances closes it.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the six balances are recoverable
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for evidence the auditor can obtain independently
options.why: SA 580 makes a representation insufficient on its own, and recoverability is a different question from existence anyway. Subsequent receipts would settle both.

items.scenario: You send positive confirmation requests to twenty customers. Six do not reply, despite two follow-ups. Those six balances total ₹1.6 crore against performance materiality of ₹40 lakh.

items.stem: What do you have to do about the opening inventory figure?

options.text: Obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether it contains misstatements that materially affect the current year
options.why: SA 510 makes opening balances the incoming auditor's responsibility to the extent they affect the current period. Opening inventory flows straight into current-year cost of sales, so a misstatement in it misstates this year's profit even though the balance itself was struck last year.

options.text: Accept the figure, because the predecessor auditor issued an unmodified opinion on it
options.misconception: treats the previous auditor's opinion as evidence for the incoming auditor
options.why: Another auditor's opinion is not audit evidence for you. Reading the predecessor's working papers may help you obtain evidence, but the unmodified opinion by itself does not discharge the requirement.

options.text: Qualify the opinion, since you did not observe the previous year's physical inventory count
options.misconception: goes straight to a modification without first trying to obtain the evidence
options.why: A modification arises only if sufficient appropriate evidence cannot be obtained. Other procedures — reviewing the predecessor's papers, testing the roll-forward, examining subsequent sales — may well settle the balance without one.

options.text: Nothing, because opening balances are outside the period covered by your audit report
options.misconception: confuses the period audited with the balances that affect it
options.why: The report covers this year, and this year's figures depend on the opening balances. That dependence is exactly why SA 510 exists as a separate standard.

items.scenario: You have been appointed for the first time as auditor of a trading company for the year ended 31 March 2026. The previous year was audited by another firm, which issued an unmodified opinion. Closing inventory of the previous year, which is the opening inventory of yours, is 18 per cent of total assets.

items.stem: At which points in an audit are analytical procedures required rather than optional?

options.text: During risk assessment, and near the end of the audit when forming an overall conclusion
options.why: These are the two mandatory uses. Risk assessment analytical procedures help identify matters the auditor was not previously aware of; the ones near the end test whether the financial statements as a whole remain consistent with the auditor's understanding of the entity.

options.text: As substantive procedures for every material account balance
options.misconception: treats the optional substantive use as compulsory
options.why: Substantive analytical procedures are one permitted response to an assessed risk, chosen when the relationship being tested is plausible and predictable enough to be reliable. The auditor may instead rely entirely on tests of details.

options.text: Only near the end of the audit, when forming an overall conclusion
options.misconception: remembers the final review and forgets the risk assessment use
options.why: The final overall review is mandatory, but so is the use during risk assessment. Omitting the planning-stage procedures loses the point at which unexpected relationships are most useful — before the audit approach has been fixed.

options.text: Only during planning, since by the end the detailed testing has already been done
options.misconception: assumes detailed testing makes the final overall review redundant
options.why: Detailed testing is done account by account. The procedures near the end look at the statements as a whole, which is a different question and one no amount of account-level testing answers.

items.stem: How do you use the ₹5 lakh you found?

options.text: Project it across the population, and compare the projected misstatement against performance materiality
options.why: SA 530 requires projection. The ₹5 lakh was found in a sample representing ₹40 crore, so it is evidence about the whole balance. Projected on value, ₹5 lakh in ₹2 crore scales to about ₹1 crore across ₹40 crore — well past the ₹60 lakh threshold, which the raw ₹5 lakh would have hidden completely.

options.text: Treat ₹5 lakh as the misstatement, since that is the only error actually identified
options.misconception: treats a sample result as if it were a complete examination
options.why: That is the error the whole standard exists to prevent. Testing 5 per cent of the value and reporting only what that 5 per cent contained understates the population by construction.

options.text: Ignore it, because ₹5 lakh is below performance materiality
options.misconception: compares an unprojected sample error against a population-level threshold
options.why: Performance materiality applies to the population. Comparing an unprojected sample error against it puts the two on different scales, and a large population misstatement passes.

options.text: Extend the sample to all 2,000 balances before concluding
options.misconception: abandons sampling at the first error rather than using its result
options.why: Testing the whole population is always available but is not the required response to finding an error. SA 530 asks the auditor to project first; the projected figure, together with the reason for the errors, is what decides whether more work is needed.

items.scenario: Trade receivables total ₹40 crore across 2,000 balances. You select a sample of 100 balances totalling ₹2 crore and find overstatements of ₹5 lakh within it. Performance materiality is ₹60 lakh.

items.stem: What does SA 550 require beyond checking the disclosure?

options.text: Treat it as a significant risk, inspect the underlying agreement, and evaluate whether the business rationale suggests fraud
options.why: Lending money is outside the normal course of business for a pump manufacturer, the amount is significant, and the counterparty is related. SA 550 makes that combination a significant risk and asks specifically whether the rationale points to fraudulent reporting or concealed misappropriation.

options.text: Nothing further, because the transaction has been identified and disclosed in the related party note
options.misconception: treats correct disclosure as the whole of the auditor's responsibility
options.why: Disclosure is one requirement. It says nothing about whether the transaction is what it appears to be, which is the question a significant risk obliges the auditor to answer.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the loan was on arm's length terms
options.misconception: relies on a representation to settle a matter it cannot settle
options.why: Under SA 580 a written representation is never sufficient appropriate evidence on its own. Here it would substitute management's word for the very rationale under examination — and the terms described are plainly not arm's length.

options.text: Report the loan to those charged with governance and take no further audit action
options.misconception: mistakes communicating a matter for auditing it
options.why: Communication is required and is not the response. SA 550 asks for inspection of the contract and an evaluation of the rationale, which is audit work rather than reporting.

items.scenario: A company that manufactures pumps lends ₹9 crore, interest free and repayable on demand, to a partnership firm in which the managing director's spouse is a partner. The company has never made a loan to anyone before. The loan is disclosed in the related party note.

items.stem: What is the effect of dual dating on your responsibility?

options.text: Responsibility for events after 20 May is limited to the amendment described
options.why: SA 560 permits an additional date restricted to the amendment, which confines the auditor's procedures on subsequent events for the period after the original report date to that amendment. Without dual dating, the later date would carry responsibility for everything up to it.

options.text: Responsibility extends to all events occurring up to 4 June
options.misconception: describes the effect of simply re-dating the report, which is the alternative the auditor did not take
options.why: Re-dating the whole report to 4 June would carry that consequence and would require subsequent-events procedures up to the new date. Dual dating exists so that the auditor may avoid it.

options.text: Dual dating is not permitted once the report has been issued to management
options.misconception: invents a bar on dual dating that the Standard does not contain
options.why: SA 560 addresses amendments made before the financial statements are issued and expressly provides for the additional date. Nothing turns on whether a draft reached management.

options.text: Dual dating requires the entire report to be reissued with fresh procedures on all subsequent events
options.misconception: requires the full procedures that dual dating is designed to avoid
options.why: Extending procedures to all subsequent events up to the new date is what re-dating requires. Dual dating restricts the procedures to the amendment, which is its whole purpose.

items.scenario: Your report on the 31 March financial statements is dated 20 May. On 4 June, before the statements are issued, a major debtor is declared insolvent. Management amends the financial statements for that event alone, and you amend your report using dual dating.

items.stem: How should your report deal with this?

options.text: Unmodified opinion, with a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern"
options.why: SA 570 (Revised) requires exactly this when a material uncertainty exists and is adequately disclosed: the opinion stays unmodified and a separate, specifically headed section draws attention to the disclosure.

options.text: Qualified opinion, because a material uncertainty exists
options.misconception: treats the existence of uncertainty as itself a reason to modify
options.why: Adequate disclosure of an uncertainty is not a misstatement. The opinion is modified only if the disclosure is inadequate — which is the opposite of these facts.

options.text: Unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph
options.misconception: reaches for the general emphasis paragraph where a specific required section exists
options.why: SA 570 (Revised) replaced the emphasis-paragraph treatment with a dedicated, separately headed section. Using SA 706 here omits the heading the standard requires.

options.text: Disclaimer of opinion, because the outcome cannot be predicted
options.misconception: confuses an uncertain future outcome with an inability to obtain evidence
options.why: Evidence about management's assessment was available and was obtained. SA 570 contemplates a disclaimer only in multiple-uncertainty situations of an altogether different order.

items.scenario: A client has recurring losses and a net current liability position. Management's going concern assessment concludes the entity remains a going concern, discloses the circumstances and the material uncertainty adequately in the notes, and you agree with that assessment.

items.stem: How should your report deal with this?

options.text: An unmodified opinion, with a separate Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section drawing attention to the note
options.why: The basis is appropriate and the disclosure is adequate, so there is nothing wrong with the financial statements and the opinion stands unmodified. SA 570 (Revised) then requires a separate section under that heading, pointing to the note and stating that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.

options.text: A qualified opinion, because a material uncertainty exists
options.misconception: modifies the opinion for an uncertainty the accounts have properly disclosed
options.why: A modification says something is wrong with the financial statements. Here they are right — they disclose the uncertainty exactly as they should. Qualifying would penalise good disclosure.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph
options.misconception: uses the general Emphasis of Matter where the standard gives a dedicated section
options.why: Before the revision this was the treatment. SA 570 (Revised) replaced it with a section under its own heading, so that going concern uncertainty is found in the same place in every report rather than among other emphasised matters.

options.text: An adverse opinion, because the company cannot pay its debts
options.misconception: treats financial difficulty itself as a misstatement
options.why: An adverse opinion is for financial statements that are materially and pervasively wrong. A company in difficulty whose accounts say so honestly is the case for which the going concern section exists.

items.scenario: A company has net current liabilities of ₹56 crore and has defaulted on a term loan. The directors have prepared the accounts on a going concern basis relying on a letter of support from the parent, and the notes describe the default, the reliance and the uncertainty in full. You are satisfied the going concern basis is appropriate but that a material uncertainty exists.

items.stem: What is wrong with relying on the representation letter here?

options.text: Written representations are never sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about the matters they cover
options.why: SA 580 says this in terms. The letter is evidence, and its absence would itself be a problem, but it does not replace procedures on related parties. That management asserts something is precisely what the audit exists to test.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because management is responsible for the disclosures and has confirmed them in writing
options.misconception: treats management's own assertion as verification of that assertion
options.why: Management's responsibility for the financial statements is what creates the need for an audit; it does not discharge it. A representation restates the assertion under audit rather than corroborating it.

options.text: The letter should have been obtained from those charged with governance instead
options.misconception: confuses who signs the letter with what the letter can prove
options.why: Who signs it is a separate requirement, and the letter is properly requested from management with appropriate responsibilities for the financial statements. Changing the signatory would not make the representation sufficient evidence.

options.text: The letter is only valid if dated the same day as the auditor's report
options.misconception: substitutes a dating rule for the sufficiency question
options.why: Dating matters — representations are dated as near as practicable to, but not after, the date of the auditor's report — but a correctly dated letter is still not sufficient appropriate evidence on its own.

items.scenario: Management has signed a representation letter confirming that all related party transactions have been disclosed. You have performed no other procedures on related parties, on the basis that the letter covers the point.

items.stem: How does your audit report deal with the three branches?

options.text: It states the division of responsibility, giving the magnitude of the portion audited by the other auditors
options.why: SA 600 has the principal auditor disclose that part of the entity was audited by others and how large that part is. The reader then knows how much of the opinion rests on work the principal auditor did not perform.

options.text: It says nothing, because the principal auditor's opinion covers the whole company
options.misconception: treats silence as the way to give a single undivided opinion
options.why: The opinion does cover the whole company, and that is exactly why the division has to be disclosed. Saying nothing leaves the reader assuming the principal auditor did all of it.

options.text: It excludes the three branches from the scope of the opinion
options.misconception: confuses dividing responsibility with limiting the scope of the opinion
options.why: The opinion is on the financial statements as a whole. Carving out branches would leave an opinion on part of a set of accounts, which is not what is being reported on.

options.text: It names each of the three other firms and reproduces their opinions
options.misconception: substitutes attaching other reports for stating the division
options.why: What SA 600 asks for is the magnitude of the divided portion, not a compendium of other reports. Reproducing them would not tell the reader how much of the whole they represent.

items.scenario: You are the auditor of a company with four branches. Three are audited by other firms, whose reports you have received and reviewed. Those three branches account for 46 per cent of total assets and 39 per cent of revenue.

items.stem: To what extent may you use internal auditors to provide direct assistance on the audit?

options.text: Not at all — the Standard does not permit direct assistance
options.why: SA 610 (Revised) as issued in India does not permit the external auditor to use internal auditors to provide direct assistance. The external auditor may still use the work of the internal audit function, which is a different thing.

options.text: For any area, provided the external auditor directs, supervises and reviews the work
options.misconception: applies the international standard's direct-assistance regime, which India did not adopt
options.why: The direction-supervision-review conditions belong to a version of the standard that permits direct assistance. The Indian SA 610 (Revised) removes the permission entirely, so the conditions never arise.

options.text: Only for areas of low assessed risk of material misstatement
options.misconception: treats a prohibition as a risk-graded restriction
options.why: The prohibition is not calibrated to risk. Low risk does not create a permission the Standard does not give.

options.text: Only with the written consent of those charged with governance
options.misconception: assumes governance consent can authorise what the Standard forbids
options.why: Those charged with governance cannot waive a requirement of the Standards. Consent is irrelevant to a prohibition.

citation.ref: para 5 and the Indian scope limitation

items.stem: How should the valuer's involvement be reflected in your audit report?

options.text: Not mentioned at all, unless law or regulation requires it
options.why: SA 620 keeps the expert out of the report by default. Naming them invites the reader to think responsibility has been divided, when the auditor's responsibility for the opinion is undiminished.

options.text: Named in the Basis for Opinion section, to show which part of the evidence came from an expert
options.misconception: treats a reference to the expert as a helpful disclosure rather than a misleading one
options.why: A voluntary reference suggests the opinion rests partly on someone else. SA 620 permits a reference only where law or regulation requires it, and then only with a statement that it does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

options.text: Named, with a statement that responsibility for the land valuation rests with the valuer
options.misconception: believes responsibility can be transferred to the expert by disclosing them
options.why: This is the opposite of what SA 620 says. The auditor's responsibility for the opinion is sole, and no wording in the report can move part of it to an expert.

options.text: Mentioned as a Key Audit Matter, since an expert was needed
options.misconception: treats the use of an expert as itself a Key Audit Matter
options.why: Key Audit Matters are the matters of most significance in the audit, selected from those communicated to those charged with governance. Engaging an expert may accompany such a matter but does not create one.

items.scenario: You engage a registered valuer to value a plot of land carried at ₹22 crore. The valuer's report supports the carrying amount. You are satisfied with the valuer's competence, capabilities and objectivity, and with the reasonableness of the assumptions used.

items.stem: In what order do the first two sections of an auditor's report appear under SA 700 (Revised)?

options.text: Opinion, then Basis for Opinion
options.why: The revised reporting standards deliberately put the conclusion first. Basis for Opinion follows immediately, and includes the statement that the auditor is independent and has fulfilled the other ethical responsibilities.

options.text: Basis for Opinion, then Opinion
options.misconception: assumes reasons must precede a conclusion, as in the pre-revision format
options.why: This was the older shape, where the reader worked through scope and basis before reaching the opinion. The revision reversed it precisely because the opinion is what readers came for.

options.text: Key Audit Matters, then Opinion
options.misconception: promotes Key Audit Matters above the opinion itself
options.why: Key Audit Matters appear later in the report, and only where SA 701 applies. They explain what most occupied the auditor; they never displace the opinion from first position.

options.text: Management's Responsibilities, then Opinion
options.misconception: opens with whose duty it is rather than with what was concluded
options.why: The responsibilities sections sit well below the opinion and basis. Opening with them would bury the conclusion behind material the reader already assumes.

items.stem: For which audits is a Key Audit Matters section required?

options.text: Audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and where law or the engagement terms otherwise require it
options.why: SA 701 applies to audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, to circumstances where the auditor is otherwise required by law or regulation to communicate key audit matters, and where the auditor decides to do so voluntarily.

options.text: Every audit, whatever the entity
options.misconception: extends a listed-entity requirement to all audits
options.why: SA 701 states its scope narrowly. For an unlisted entity the auditor may communicate key audit matters, but is not required to.

options.text: Every audit, because the section replaces the basis-for-opinion section
options.misconception: treats key audit matters as a replacement for a section that remains required in every report
